title: A Saturday at the market
paragraphs: Every Saturday, Efua goes to the big market in the city centre. She usually leaves home at seven o'clock, before the streets get busy. She takes a shared taxi because it is cheaper than a private one.

At the market, she buys vegetables, fish and rice for the whole week. She always visits the same seller, Mrs Agbo, because her tomatoes are fresh and her prices are fair. They often chat about their families.

This Saturday is different. Efua is not shopping for food. She is looking for a present for her brother, who is graduating next week. After an hour, she finds a beautiful leather bag. It is expensive, but she decides to buy it. "He will use it every day at his new job," she thinks.

title: How mobile money changed daily life
paragraphs: Twenty years ago, sending money to a relative in another town was slow and risky. People often gave cash to a bus driver or travelled for hours to deliver it themselves. Today, in many West African countries, a few taps on a basic phone are enough.

Mobile money services allow users to store money in an account linked to their phone number. They can transfer it, pay bills or buy airtime without a bank account. This has been especially important for people in rural areas, where banks are rare and often far away.

Researchers have found that families who use mobile money are better able to deal with emergencies, such as an illness or a poor harvest, because relatives can send help quickly. Small traders also benefit: they can receive payments from customers they have never met.

However, the system is not perfect. Transaction fees can be high for small amounts, and fraud — for example, fake messages asking users to send money back — remains a problem. Experts argue that better digital education is as important as new technology.

title: Why sleep helps you learn
paragraphs: Many students believe that staying up late is the best way to prepare for an exam. Scientific studies suggest the opposite: sleep plays an essential role in learning.

During the day, the brain collects new information. At night, especially during deep sleep, it reorganises this information and transfers important memories to long-term storage. In one well-known type of experiment, people who slept after learning a list of words remembered more of them the next day than people who stayed awake.
Sleep also affects attention. After a short night, it is harder to concentrate, and we make more mistakes. This is why a tired student may read the same page several times without understanding it.
For language learners, the message is clear: regular short study sessions followed by a good night's sleep are more effective than one long session the night before a test.

title: Brain drain or brain gain?
paragraphs: Every year, thousands of young Africans leave their countries to study or work abroad. Doctors move to the United Kingdom, engineers to Canada, and students to France, Germany or China. For decades, this movement was described as a 'brain drain': the departure of talented people whose education had been paid for by their home countries, which then lost their skills.

The costs are real. In some countries, more doctors trained locally now work abroad than at home, and hospitals struggle to replace them. Governments argue that they invest heavily in universities only to see graduates contribute to the economies of richer nations. Critics add that recruitment campaigns by foreign health services make the problem worse.

However, a growing number of economists question this pessimistic view. They point out that migrants send home remittances worth more than all international aid combined, money which pays for school fees, small businesses and medical care. Moreover, the possibility of working abroad encourages more young people to pursue higher education in the first place, and not all of them actually leave.

There is also the phenomenon of 'brain circulation'. Many professionals return after several years, bringing new skills, international networks and capital. Others remain abroad but invest in start-ups, mentor students online or create partnerships between universities. In this sense, the diaspora can become a bridge rather than a loss.

Whether migration is a drain or a gain therefore depends largely on policy. Countries that offer attractive conditions for returnees, recognise foreign qualifications and involve their diaspora in development projects tend to benefit most. The question, experts conclude, is not how to stop people from leaving, but how to make sure that their success abroad also benefits those who stay.

drain.def: a continuous loss of something valuable

recruitment.def: the process of finding new people to work for an organisation

remittances.def: money sent by migrants to their families at home

pursue.def: to try to achieve something over time

returnees.def: people who come back to their country after living abroad

diaspora.def: people from one country who live in other countries

mentor.def: to advise and help a less experienced person

capital.def: money used to start or develop a business

summary: Skilled migration costs African countries talent, but remittances, returnees and diaspora networks can turn it into a gain, depending on government policy.

title: Will AI tutors replace teachers?
paragraphs: Few technologies have entered classrooms as rapidly as generative AI. Within two years of its public release, students on every continent were using chatbots to summarise readings, check grammar and, inevitably, write essays. Predictably, the debate has polarised: enthusiasts herald a revolution in personalised learning, while sceptics warn of a generation that outsources thinking itself.

The case for AI tutoring rests largely on a well-established finding. Decades of research indicate that one-to-one tutoring dramatically improves outcomes compared with conventional classroom instruction. Until now, such tutoring has been prohibitively expensive; an AI that adapts to each learner at negligible cost could, in principle, democratise it.

Yet the evidence so far is more nuanced than either camp suggests. Several studies have found that students who rely on AI to solve problems perform well during practice but worse on subsequent tests, arguably because the tool removes the productive struggle through which durable learning occurs. Where AI was configured to give hints rather than answers, however, the decline largely disappeared.

What emerges, then, is less a story of replacement than of redesign. Teachers remain indispensable for what machines do poorly: motivating reluctant learners, reading a room, and modelling intellectual curiosity. The more pressing question is not whether AI belongs in education, but how institutions can harness it without eroding the very skills education is meant to build.

outsources.def: gives work to an outside person or system

prohibitively.def: so much that people cannot afford it

negligible.def: so small it is not important

harness.def: to control and use something for a purpose

summary: AI tutoring could make one-to-one help cheap, but it harms learning when it gives answers; the future lies in redesigning teaching, not replacing teachers.

title: A weekend in Kpalimé
paragraphs: Last month, Kodjo and his friends went to Kpalimé for the weekend. They left Lomé early on Saturday morning and arrived two hours later.

In the afternoon, they climbed Mount Agou, the highest mountain in Togo. It was hot and the path was difficult, but the view from the top was amazing. They could see villages, forests and even Lake Volta in the distance.

In the evening, they stayed in a small guesthouse. The owner cooked a delicious dinner of fufu and peanut soup. On Sunday, they visited a waterfall and bought some coffee from a local farmer before they went home. Kodjo wants to go back next year.

title: Life without a phone
paragraphs: Ama is 22 and, like most young people, she uses her phone all the time. Last week, her teacher gave the class a challenge: no phone for three days.
The first day was very hard. Ama didn't know the time, she couldn't check the news and she missed her friends' messages. She felt bored and a little nervous.

But on the second day, things got better. She read a book, went for a walk and talked to her neighbours. On the third day, she slept better and had more time to study. "I'm not going to stop using my phone," she says, "but now I switch it off every evening at nine."

title: Why young people volunteer
paragraphs: Every Saturday, Sena, a 24-year-old accountant, spends four hours teaching reading to children in a community centre in Lomé. She isn't paid, but she says it is the best part of her week.

Sena is one of a growing number of young Africans who volunteer. Some help in hospitals, others clean beaches or teach computer skills. According to a recent survey, more than a third of young people in the region have volunteered at least once in the past year.

Their reasons vary. Many want to give something back to their community. Others see volunteering as a way to gain experience, meet new people and improve their CV. "Employers often ask me about it in interviews," says Sena.

However, volunteering is not always easy. Organisations sometimes lack money and volunteers can find it hard to balance their free time with work or studies. Experts suggest that short, flexible projects are the best way to keep young volunteers involved.

title: Is your phone stealing your sleep?
paragraphs: Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep a night, yet surveys consistently show that a large proportion of young people get far less. While stress and long working hours play a part, researchers increasingly point to another culprit: the smartphone.

The problem is twofold. First, the blue light emitted by screens suppresses melatonin, the hormone that tells the body it is time to sleep. Second, and perhaps more importantly, phones keep the brain alert: an exciting video, a worrying message or an endless social media feed makes it much harder to switch off.

The consequences go beyond feeling tired. Chronic lack of sleep has been linked to poorer concentration, weaker memory and a higher risk of depression. For students preparing for exams, this is particularly worrying, since much of what we learn during the day is consolidated while we sleep.

Fortunately, the solutions are simple, if not always easy. Experts recommend putting the phone away at least an hour before bed, keeping it out of the bedroom and using an old-fashioned alarm clock. Those who try it often report falling asleep faster within a week.

culprit.def: the person or thing responsible for a problem

summary: Smartphones harm sleep through blue light and mental stimulation, which affects memory and mood; keeping the phone away before bed helps quickly.

title: Solar power in West Africa
paragraphs: Across West Africa, millions of homes still have no reliable electricity. Extending the national grid to remote villages is slow and expensive, which is why a growing number of communities are turning to an alternative that is literally above their heads: the sun.

Off-grid solar kits, consisting of a small panel, a battery and a few lights, have become dramatically cheaper over the past decade. Many are sold on a pay-as-you-go basis: customers pay a small amount each day by mobile money, and after a year or two the system is theirs.

The benefits are considerable. Children can study after dark without breathing in smoke from kerosene lamps, small shops can stay open longer, and farmers can charge their phones to check market prices. Some health centres now use solar power to keep vaccines cold.

Nevertheless, challenges remain. Cheap, low-quality equipment sometimes breaks within months, and recycling old batteries is a growing environmental problem. Analysts argue that governments should set quality standards and support local repair businesses if solar power is to fulfil its promise.

off-grid.def: not connected to the main electricity network

summary: Cheap pay-as-you-go solar kits bring light and power to villages without electricity, but quality and battery recycling need regulation.

title: Do endangered languages matter?
paragraphs: Linguists estimate that roughly half of the world's seven thousand languages may cease to be spoken by the end of this century. Most of these have few speakers, no written tradition and little presence in schools or the media. As older speakers die and younger generations shift to dominant languages, entire ways of describing the world disappear with them.

Sceptics argue that this is simply the natural course of history: languages have always risen and fallen, and a common language facilitates trade, education and mobility. Why, they ask, should scarce public funds be spent preserving tongues that their own speakers are abandoning?

Proponents of revitalisation offer several counter-arguments. Languages encode irreplaceable knowledge, from the medicinal properties of local plants to sophisticated systems of navigation. Moreover, there is growing evidence that children who are first taught to read in their mother tongue go on to perform better, including in the dominant language, than those immersed in an unfamiliar one from day one.

Perhaps the most compelling case, however, is a matter of dignity rather than utility. For many communities, a language is inseparable from identity, and its loss is experienced as a profound injustice. The debate, then, is less about whether diversity has value than about who should bear the cost of sustaining it.

title: The fifteen-minute city
paragraphs: The idea is deceptively simple: residents should be able to reach most of their daily needs — work, school, shops, healthcare, green space — within a fifteen-minute walk or bike ride. Popularised by the urbanist Carlos Moreno and adopted, in various forms, by cities from Paris to Melbourne, the 'fifteen-minute city' promises cleaner air, stronger communities and less time wasted in traffic.

Its appeal is understandable. Commuting consumes hours of people's lives and a substantial share of their income, while car-dependent suburbs isolate those who cannot drive. Bringing services closer to homes, proponents argue, would benefit the elderly, children and low-income households most of all.

Critics, however, raise practical and political objections. Retrofitting sprawling cities is enormously expensive, and improving a neighbourhood can drive up rents, pushing out the very residents it was meant to help. A vocal minority has even portrayed the concept as a plot to restrict movement, a claim urban planners firmly reject.

For rapidly growing African cities, the debate takes on a different character. Many neighbourhoods already function informally as fifteen-minute cities, with markets, schools and workshops within walking distance. The challenge may be less to impose a new model than to protect and upgrade what already works.

deceptively.def: in a way that seems different from reality

commuting.def: travelling regularly between home and work

retrofitting.def: adding new features to something old

sprawling.def: spreading over a large area in an untidy way

summary: The fifteen-minute city aims to put daily needs within walking distance; critics cite cost and rising rents, while African cities may already work this way informally.
